1: Job is a good and wealthy man. Satan claims he serves God only because he is blessed, and God permits a test. In one day Job loses his herds, servants and all ten children. He says, "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord."
The book asks whether anyone loves God for his own sake.
2: Satan is allowed to afflict Job with sores from head to foot. His wife tells him to curse God and die. Three friends come and sit with him in silence for seven days.
"Shall we receive good from God and not evil?" The friends' silence is the best thing they do.
3: Job curses the day he was born
Job breaks the silence, wishing he had never been born and asking why life is given to those in misery.
Scripture gives words to deep grief. Job does not curse God.
4: Eliphaz: the innocent do not perish
Eliphaz gently argues that no innocent person was ever destroyed, so Job must have done something.
The friends' theory: suffering always means guilt. The book will reject it.
5: He urges Job to turn to God, who wounds and also heals.
True in general, wrong about Job.
6: Job: my grief is heavier than sand
Job says his words are wild because his pain is real, and that his friends have failed him like a dried-up stream.
Suffering people need loyalty before arguments.
7: Life is hard service, and his days pass without hope. He asks God, "Why have you made me your target?"
Job takes his complaint directly to God.
8: Bildad says God does not pervert justice; if Job were pure, God would restore him.
Bluntly implies that Job's children deserved their fate.
9: Job: who can argue with God?
Job agrees God is mighty but sees no way to bring his case. He wishes there were a mediator between them.
Christians hear this longing answered in Christ.
10: Job: why did you make me?
Job asks God why he formed him with such care only to destroy him.
Job holds on to the fact that God made him.
11: Zophar says God is exacting less than Job's guilt deserves.
12: Job answers with sarcasm: "No doubt wisdom will die with you." Everyone knows God is powerful.
13: Job calls his friends worthless physicians and resolves to argue his case with God. "Though he slay me, I will trust in him."
Faith and protest in the same breath.
14: Human life is short and full of trouble. A tree cut down may sprout again, but will a man who dies live again?
Job reaches toward a hope beyond death.
15: Now he accuses Job of undermining religion and describes the terrors of the wicked.
The friends grow harsher as their theory fails.
16: Job says he could talk the same way in their place. Even now, he says, "my witness is in heaven".
He appeals to God against God's apparent treatment of him.
17: Job sees nothing ahead but the grave.
The low point of his hope.
18: Bildad on the fate of the wicked
A vivid picture of the wicked man's ruin, aimed at Job.
Accurate about evil, wrong about the man in front of him.
19: I know that my Redeemer lives
Job feels abandoned by family and friends. Then he declares, "I know that my Redeemer lives, and in my flesh I shall see God."
One of the great statements of hope in the Old Testament.
20: Zophar: the joy of the wicked is short
He insists that ill-gotten wealth is soon vomited up.
21: Job points out that the wicked frequently live long, grow rich and die in peace.
He appeals to facts against a tidy theory.
22: He now accuses Job of specific crimes against the poor and urges him to repent.
When the theory needs sins, they are made up.
23: If only I could find him
Job longs to find God and lay out his case. "He knows the way I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold."
24: Job lists the wrongs done to the poor and asks why God does not set times for judgement.
The problem of evil stated honestly.
25: A short speech: how can a mortal be righteous before God?
The friends have run out of arguments.
26: Job himself describes God's majesty over sea and sky. These are only the outskirts of his ways.
Job knows God's greatness better than his friends do.
27: I will hold fast my integrity
Job swears he will not admit to sins he did not commit.
Honesty before God matters more than a quick peace.
28: People mine silver and gold from deep in the earth, but wisdom cannot be dug up or bought. God alone knows the way to it.
"The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom."
29: The days when God watched over me
Job remembers when he was respected and was eyes to the blind and a father to the poor.
30: Young men mock him, his body wastes away, and God does not answer.
The contrast with the last chapter is the measure of his loss.
31: Job reviews his life: no lust, no dishonesty, no neglect of servants or the poor, no trust in gold. He signs his defence.
A portrait of Old Testament goodness, including purity of heart.
32: A young bystander, Elihu, is angry with Job for justifying himself and with the friends for failing to answer.
33: God warns people in dreams and through pain, to turn them back from the pit.
Suffering can be medicine, not only punishment.
34: He defends God's justice and rebukes Job for speaking as if God were unfair.
He is right about God and too hard on Job.
35: Human sin or goodness does not add to or take from God.
God does not need us, which is why his care is pure gift.
36: God is mighty and does not despise anyone; he opens ears through adversity.
A step closer to the truth than the three friends.
37: Elihu describes thunder, snow and lightning as a storm approaches.
The storm prepares for God's own voice.
38: The Lord answers from the whirlwind
"Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" God questions Job about sea, dawn, snow and stars.
God does not explain; he shows who he is.
39: God asks about the mountain goat, the wild donkey, the ostrich, the war horse and the hawk. Job answers that he will put his hand over his mouth.
Creation is full of things beyond human use or understanding, all cared for by God.
40: God speaks again from the whirlwind: "Will you condemn me to justify yourself?" He describes the mighty Behemoth.
God presses the question of who is judging whom.
41: God describes Leviathan, a sea monster no one can tame.
If Job cannot face this creature, how could he judge its Maker?
42: Job says, "I had heard of you, but now my eye sees you," and repents in dust and ashes. God rebukes the three friends: they did not speak rightly of him, as Job did. Job prays for them and is given twice what he had.
Job receives no explanation, only God himself, and that is enough.
